# The HOA Board Will Now Come to Order

## I.

**NOTICE OF VIOLATION**

**Willowbrook Estates Homeowners' Association**
**Architectural Standards & Community Compliance Division**

**Property:** 414 Briar Oak Lane, Unit/Lot 7, Phase II

**Owner(s) of Record:** Meredith L. Chen & David R. Chen

**Date of Inspection:** October 3, 2024

**Violation Code:** Section 6.2(b)(iii) — Unauthorized Structural Modification to Front Façade

**Description of Violation:** Upon routine visual inspection conducted October 2, 2024, a non-approved structural addition was observed at the above-referenced property, consisting of an inclined wooden platform structure extending approximately fourteen (14) feet from the front entry threshold to the public sidewalk approach, affixed to the existing concrete stoop by means of permanent bolting. Said structure was erected without prior submission of an Architectural Modification Request (Form AMR-7), without review by the Architectural Standards Subcommittee, and without the requisite two-thirds approval vote of the Board of Directors, in violation of the procedures set forth in Sections 6.1(a), 6.2(b)(iii), and 6.4(a)(2) of the Willowbrook Estates CC&Rs.

**Remediation Window:** Fourteen (14) calendar days from date of notice.

**Fine Schedule:** Upon expiration of the remediation window without cure, a fine of $50.00 per day shall be assessed to the homeowner account, compounding on the first day of each calendar month, until such time as the violation is cured or a variance is granted through the appropriate process.

**Questions?** Please don't hesitate to reach out! We're here to help.

Warm regards,

*Doug Whitmore*
President, Willowbrook Estates HOA Board of Directors

---

The smiley face was drawn into the descending loop of the *g*. A small, careful circle with two dots for eyes, a curve for a mouth. It had been added after the signature, in the same blue ink, and it managed—through some alchemy of penmanship—to look both cheerful and institutional, as though friendliness itself were a bylaw.

Meredith stood on the ramp in her slippers. The October air was the particular cool of a Virginia morning that hadn't decided what it was yet, and she held her coffee in her left hand while her right hand held the notice, which had been affixed to the front door with a piece of painter's tape—blue, the gentle kind, designed not to damage surfaces. She read the notice once and then read it again.

The ramp beneath her feet was built of pressure-treated pine, twenty-eight inches wide at the landing, thirty-six inches wide along the run, sloping at precisely one inch of rise per twelve inches of length—gentler than the ADA required, because Kevin had looked it up and decided his father deserved gentler. Her son had constructed it over the second weekend in September, driving down from Fredericksburg in the truck he couldn't really afford with lumber he absolutely couldn't afford, and he'd worked from Saturday morning to Sunday dusk, and when he'd finished he'd stood back and said, "It's not pretty, Mom," and she'd said, "It's beautiful," and neither of them had been wrong. Kevin had added the non-slip adhesive strips himself, cutting them with a utility knife, pressing each one down with the heel of his hand. They were a dark sandy grit, the color of wet tea leaves. They were slightly uneven. One of them was already peeling at the corner.

The notice did not contain the word *wheelchair*. It did not contain the word *ramp*. It said *inclined wooden platform structure*. It did not contain the word *illness* or the word *husband* or the word *paralysis* or the word *person*.

Meredith read the fine schedule a third time. The coffee in her left hand had been hot when she'd stepped outside to retrieve the newspaper, which she'd never gotten to, because the notice was on the door.

Fifty dollars per day. Compounding monthly. No cap.

She noticed this the way she had noticed things for forty-one years at Pacific Mutual and then at its various successor entities through three mergers and a bankruptcy: structurally, involuntarily, the way a doctor at a dinner party cannot help but notice the mole on a stranger's neck. The fine structure was poorly designed. It was not designed, actually—it was borrowed, probably from a template purchased online by someone who did not understand what compound meant when attached to the word *daily*. In the first month, the fines alone would total $1,500. By the end of the second month, with compounding, $3,243. She ran the series forward in her head the way other people hummed, almost absently: at fourteen months the cumulative liability would exceed $60,000, which was roughly what she and David still owed on the mortgage, and at approximately 1.7 years—call it twenty months—the total fines would surpass the most recent assessed value of the property. $287,000. A three-bedroom ranch with original hardwood and a half-bath conversion that David had done himself in 2009, when he could still grip a wrench.

One point seven years.

She didn't know how long David had. She refused to assign a number to it. She had spent four decades assigning dollar values to the probability of death—the probability that a fifty-five-year-old nonsmoking male in good health would die within ten years (6.7%), the probability that a life insurance portfolio of ten thousand such men would produce no fewer than six hundred claims in a given decade (94.2%), the elaborate and heartless beauty of large numbers canceling out the chaos of individual fates—and she understood in a way that was cellular, that preceded thought, that the only number she had ever refused to calculate was the one that mattered. She would not run the actuarial table on her own husband. She would not. Other people's husbands. Other people's fathers and mothers and wives. All those elegant columns of the probably-dead. Never David.

But the fine had no cap, and the fine compounded, and the ramp could not come down because David needed the ramp to leave the house and David needed to leave the house because David was a sixty-eight-year-old man who had coached Little League and built a half-bath and sung, off-key and with unearnable confidence, the entirety of "American Pie" at three consecutive Fourth of July block parties, and he was not going to spend what remained of his time trapped in a building by a piece of paper.

She looked at the smiley face one more time.

Then she went inside. The coffee was cold. She poured it out and started a new cup, and while the kettle heated, she opened her laptop and began to type.

---

## II.

Linda Hwang was pricing toner cartridges when Meredith found her. The copy shop was called FastPrint Solutions, which was the kind of name generated by committee or algorithm, and it occupied a narrow storefront between a nail salon and an insurance agency in the Willowbrook Commons shopping center, a half-mile from the development's north gate. The air inside smelled of warm ink and the peculiar vanilla of recycled paper. Linda stood behind the counter in a blue polo shirt with the company logo over her heart, and when she saw Meredith she did something complicated with her face—a smile that began as genuine welcome and then, halfway through, remembered that it had reasons to be cautious.

"Meredith. Hi."

"I need to talk to you about something."

"If it's the color matching on the real estate flyers, that was Marcus, I told him—"

"It's not about flyers."

They sat in the back, on two rolling chairs between a defunct laminator and cases of paper stacked head-high. Meredith laid the violation notice on the table between them. Linda read it with the particular attention of someone who had spent seventeen years as a court stenographer in the Fairfax County Circuit Court—every word registered, every euphemism decoded, every structural evasion catalogued in a mind that had been trained to record language with the precision of a seismograph.

"Inclined wooden platform structure," Linda said.

"Yes."

"They mean the ramp."

"They mean the ramp."

Linda set the notice down. She aligned its edges with the edge of the table, an unconscious habit, the need for things to be square. "What do you want, Meredith?"

"I want you to take minutes at the annual meeting."

Something shifted behind Linda's eyes. Not quite a flinch. A calibration. "There's already a secretary. Janet Kowalski."

"Janet Kowalski takes minutes like a second grader takes notes on a field trip. 'We went to the pumpkin patch. It was fun. Doug said some stuff about mulch.' I don't need that. I need a record."

"A *record*."

"A real one. Verbatim. Every motion, every second, every ruling from the chair, every point of order. I need someone who can capture what actually happens in that room with enough fidelity that it can't be rewritten afterward."

Linda was quiet for a long time. A customer came in and the bell above the door chimed and Marcus, unseen, said, "Welcome to FastPrint Solutions, we'll be right with you." Two industrial printers hummed their overlapping hums.

"You know what happened to me," Linda said.

"I know what I've heard."

"The transcript. People say I altered a transcript."

"Did you?"

Linda looked at the cases of paper stacked against the wall. Five thousand sheets per case. The math of it, the sheer volume of blankness waiting to become someone's words.

"There was a custody hearing," she said. "A father. He was—there was a moment where the judge said something off the record. Told the father he should consider himself lucky the court didn't refer him for criminal investigation. But it was off the record. It wouldn't appear in the transcript. It wouldn't exist."

"And you put it in."

"I put it in because it happened. Because the judge *said it* and the father *heard it* and the mother sitting twelve feet away needed it to *exist* in the document that would determine whether that man got unsupervised weekends with her children. I put it in because the record is supposed to be *what happened*."

"And then."

"And then the judge found out. And the judge had been on the bench for twenty-two years and had never been contradicted by a stenographer, and the Virginia Board of—it doesn't matter. I was terminated. I wasn't disbarred. Stenographers don't get disbarred. I was *terminated*, and the board sent a letter to every court in the Commonwealth saying I was *unreliable*, which in my profession is the same as being dead." She smoothed the edges of the violation notice again. "So yes. I know something about the gap between the official record and what actually happens."

"I'm not asking you to alter anything," Meredith said. "I'm asking you to record everything. Perfectly. Completely. Every word that comes out of Doug Whitmore's mouth, captured in real time, so that when the meeting is over there is a document that cannot be disputed."

"Why?"

Meredith told her.

Linda listened. When Meredith was finished, Linda pulled the violation notice toward her one more time and read the fine schedule again, and Meredith watched her do the same math she herself had done on the ramp—not the injustice, the accumulation of it—and when Linda looked up her expression had changed. It was the expression of a woman who had been punished for making a record too accurate and who now, seven years later, was being asked to do the one thing she was singularly, damningly good at.

"I'll need a laptop," Linda said. "Not a steno machine. I don't have access to one anymore. But I can do 180 words per minute on a standard keyboard if I use the Stein method."

"I'll get you a laptop."

"And I want to be positioned where I can see the speaker's face. Punctuation depends on inflection. You'd be amazed how much a comma matters."

"I know how much a comma matters," Meredith said. "I used to calculate how much a comma matters, in dollars."

Something almost like a smile crossed Linda's face. "All right," she said. "All right."

---

Gerald Mortimer was in his usual chair on the third floor of the Willowbrook branch of the Fairfax County Public Library, in the 060s—General Organizations and Museum Science—which was the most deserted section of any public library in the country, in Gerald's informed opinion, and therefore the most conducive to focused study. He was seated with his posture arranged as precisely as a drafting instrument—spine perpendicular to seat, elbows at right angles, the book centered on the table before him—and he was reading *Robert's Rules of Order Newly Revised*, 12th edition, published 2020, 714 pages, which he later admitted to Meredith was his eleventh complete reading.

"Eleven times," Meredith said, standing across the table from him with her purse over one arm and her reading glasses pushed up into her hair.

"Twelve by Christmas, if I keep this pace."

"Gerald, why?"

He looked up at her with the mild, blinking expression of a man who has been asked why he breathes. Gerald Mortimer was seventy-one years old, retired from a career in quality assurance at a defense contractor that made components for components of systems he was not cleared to fully understand, and he possessed a mind of extraordinary orderliness that had been, for most of his professional life, applied to objects of extraordinary tedium. He was thin and tall and wore sweaters that his late wife had picked out for him a decade ago, and they were all in muted earth tones, and they all still fit perfectly, because Gerald was a man who did not change.

"Because it works," he said simply. "If you follow the rules, the meeting works. Every person gets heard. Every motion gets its due. The minority is protected. The majority decides. It's—" He paused, searching for a word, and what he landed on surprised Meredith. "It's *kind*. The whole system is an act of kindness. Henry Martyn Robert designed it because he watched a church meeting fall apart in 1863, Meredith. A *church meeting*. Good people, faithful people, and they couldn't conduct business without screaming at each other, because there were no rules. And he thought: there must be a better way. And he spent the rest of his life writing it down."

"I need that system," Meredith said.

"You need it for what?"

She sat down across from him and told him about the ramp and the fine and the smiley face in the *g*, and as she talked, Gerald's expression underwent a transformation that was, in its way, more dramatic than rage: his eyes narrowed with the focus of a man seeing a problem that engaged every faculty he possessed. He reached for a notepad—he always carried a notepad—and began writing before she'd finished.

"The annual meeting is November 14," he said.

"Yes."

"That's thirty-one days."

"Yes."

"What's your objective?"

"I want Doug Whitmore removed as president."

Gerald wrote this down. Then he looked at it. Then he looked at Meredith. "Robert's Rules doesn't have a specific motion called 'vote of no confidence,'" he said. "That's a parliamentary concept, British system. But there are equivalent mechanisms. You can rescind a previous election by majority vote with prior notice, or by two-thirds vote without. Or—" He flipped to a section of his book marked with a green tab. "If the bylaws allow for removal of officers. Do they?"

"I have the bylaws in my car."

"Get them."

She got them. Gerald read them at the table, all ninety-four pages, and he read them the way Meredith had read the fine schedule—not for content but for structure, for the load-bearing walls and the hollow spaces, for the provisions that held weight and the ones that crumbled when you leaned on them. It took him two hours. Meredith went downstairs to the periodicals section and read three days' worth of newspapers she'd been ignoring. When she came back, Gerald had filled seven pages of his notepad with notes in handwriting so precise it looked typeset.

"This document," he said, "is a mess."

"I know."

"Article IV says the board serves at the pleasure of the membership. Article VII says officers can only be removed for cause. Article IV supersedes Article VII by order of adoption—I can tell from the amendment dates—but nobody's going to know that. Doug certainly doesn't."

"What else?"
